I am sure you can think of other types of foods that seem more expensive than everything else.

I could buy three times as much soda at the grocery store for the same amount of money.
Why are things like soda nearly two to three times more expensive in restaurants? Some things (like tofu and avocados) seem relatively more expensive than other foods.

It's them covering the overhead. They factor in the unlimited refills, figure everybody is gonna get 2-3 over the course of a meal, and have to adjust accordingly.

The reason certain things on menus seem somewhat overpriced is generally because of either the hassle to make it, it's difficult to acquire, or they're using certain lower priced items to cover what they lose on things like, say, prawns. If you want to be able to serve those, your generally can't charge customers what you'd need in order to profit. So you sell the meal at cost, or just slightly above, and tack 50 cents here, 50 there, hey extra guac is a dollar... It's a good way of seeming high class, when you're actually middling, and making sure you keep the doors open.
Also there is little profit on food, it's drinks where most places make their money.
Yeah, that alcohol markup is just a beast.

I'm going to use fast food resturants as my example, but the same concept applies to most fountain soda resturants.Fountain soda is made from syrup bought in bulk, which brings the cost to make a 32oz soda+ice around $0.10-$0.15. Add the cost of a lid, cup, and straw, you get about $0.22/soda. This makes soda easily one of the most profitable, often-sold items. This is used by fast food resturants to keep the prices of their food low.

Here's an example: Stoner guy goes to Burger King, gets 2 $1.50 10pc nuggets with four sauce packets, and a large drink for $1.90, for a total of $4.90. $3.00/20 nuggets means you're paying about $0.15/nugget, so you can imagine the profit margin there is not great when considering the other costs of preparing the food and the cost of sauce packets which are often free. That's why the soda is so pricey, that $1.68 profit from it accounts for about 33% of the overall money spent!

Example of using soda price to maintain profit during business shifts: The McDonald's in my area offers $1 soft drinks of any size, but when buying a large combo, the drink costs $1.60. This wasn't always the case, it changed several years ago when McDonald's started to see their business plateauing and competition rising. They did this to avoid raising the cost of their food while allowing people to just buy a $1 soft drink to remain the destination for people looking for just a soda. They also use the $1 soda as an advertising point to draw people so maybe they buy a little bit more than that.

Source for numbers.
